title: “Why?” – Life’s Most Important Question. Who Are You Really Toiling For?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.
sources: Deci, Edward L., Effects of Externally Mediated Rewards on Intrinsic Motivation, “Journal of Personality and Social Psychology” 18 (1971)
Deci, Edward L.; Koestner, Richard; Ryan, Richard M., A Meta-Analytic Review of Experiments Examining the Effects of Extrinsic Rewards on Intrinsic Motivation, “Psychological Bulletin” 125 (1999)
Schwartz, Barry, Why We Work, TED Books / Simon & Schuster 2015
Wrzesniewski, Amy; Dutton, Jane E., Crafting a Job: Revisioning Employees as Active Crafters of Their Work, “Academy of Management Review” 26 (2001)

paragraphs: The American researchers Amy Wrzesniewski and Jane Dutton described conversations with people who cleaned the rooms of a large hospital. Formally they all had the same duties, and yet they talked about their work in two completely different ways. For some it was a simple, thankless job to be endured somehow until the end of the shift. Others saw themselves as part of the team that was healing patients and found time to encourage their families. One woman changed the pictures every week in the rooms of patients with brain injuries, who lay there for months on end. She wanted them to feel that going home was getting closer. Nobody had handed them this approach to work along with their uniforms. Behind these different stories lay the answer to one question: who were they doing all this for?

Nearly three thousand years earlier, a king in Jerusalem carried out an experiment on himself. The Teacher (in Hebrew, Qoheleth) built houses, laid out gardens and made reservoirs, and amassed silver and gold. He admitted that his work gave him joy (Ecclesiastes 2:4-10). In the Hebrew text of verses 4-8 the short word li (לִי), meaning “for me”, appears no fewer than eight times, which could be rendered: I built for myself, I planted for myself, I gathered for myself. Yet when he looked at the whole of his achievements, he concluded that everything was “futile, a pursuit of the wind” (Ecclesiastes 2:11). All these works had a single beneficiary: himself.

Toward the end of the same chapter, however, comes a sentence that changes the perspective. The joy of eating, drinking and working is a gift “from the hand of God” (Ecclesiastes 2:24). It is our achievements that prove fleeting, but the ability to find satisfaction in them is a gift. And the fruit of our work can serve others. Two chapters later the Teacher describes a lonely man who works without rest until at last he asks himself who he is actually toiling for (Ecclesiastes 4:8).

You can rarely change your job overnight. Far more often, though, you can notice whom your work serves. A spreadsheet can help someone get paid on time, and a clean stairwell makes it easier for a neighbor to carry her shopping in safely. A sense of meaning does not justify poor working conditions. And where it is missing, even good work can lead to burnout. The Teacher began asking about the meaning of his achievements only at the height of his success. You can ask yourself “why?” today, over an ordinary task, before you commit yourself to something more time-consuming.
Prepared by: Marek Micyk
Content editor: Beata Dutkowska

questions: Who does what I do every day matter to?
challenge: Before you put down your phone or close your computer today, choose one task that awaits you tomorrow and that you dislike. In your mind, finish the sentence: “I am doing this for…”. Fill in the blank with the name of a specific person. Think about what exactly will change in their day if you do this task well.

paragraphs: How much do you have to pay people to make them lose interest in something they enjoy? In 1971 Edward Deci, a young psychologist fresh from his doctorate at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, described an experiment suggesting that sometimes a single dollar is enough.

Students came to the laboratory for three sessions. In each one they worked on a three-dimensional puzzle: using seven plastic pieces, they had to build a shape shown in a drawing. The researcher assumed that they would find the task interesting and enjoyable, and indeed they confirmed this in a short questionnaire after each session. Halfway through each session he left the room for a few minutes, on the pretext of urgent work at the computer, and watched through a one-way mirror what the participants were doing. The latest issues of magazines lay on the table, and yet many students went on working on the puzzle.

At the first session no one was paid. During the second, half of the participants received a dollar for each shape completed within the time limit. At the third, the researcher told the group that there had been enough money for only one session, so this time there would be no payment. The result was telling: once payment was withdrawn, those who had previously been paid for the puzzles spent less time on them than before the reward was introduced. The group that had never been paid played with them even slightly longer than at the start of the study.

Nothing about the puzzle pieces had changed, after all. Only the answer to the question “Why am I doing this?” had changed. On the second day it was “for the money”, and when the money disappeared, the old “because it’s interesting” came back only in part.
If even a small reward can weaken our desire to do a task we used to enjoy, how does a salary affect our motivation for work we do for years?

sections.heading: The Dollar That Changes Your Attitude
paragraphs: In the years that followed, the study was repeated in dozens of versions: with children, with drawing, with material rewards instead of money. In 1999 the results of more than a hundred such experiments were brought together in a meta-analysis, which confirmed the original pattern. A reward promised in advance simply for completing an interesting task usually weakens the earlier desire to do it. Psychologists still argue about the details today, though there is agreement on a few points. Praise and factual feedback work quite differently from money, and with boring work payment has nothing to take away; it simply helps get the work done.

The conclusion, then, is more modest than self-help books like to suggest, but far more useful. Motivation has several levels. Some people work for a reward, others out of fear of punishment, for someone’s approval, or because the work itself matters to them. From the outside they may look the same, but the difference shows when the reward disappears or the boss goes on vacation.

Most of us know this mechanism from our own lives, though we rarely call it by name. A job we waited for a long time turns, after a year, into a list of tasks to tick off, and a passion turned into paid commissions begins to chafe. Someone played the guitar for years purely for pleasure, then began playing at weddings, and after two seasons of “wedding work” no longer touches the instrument at home. At such times we rarely ask what has actually happened to our “why?”; far more often we simply look around for the next reward. But this kind of motivation has a serious flaw: it has to be constantly fed with new incentives, and each new reward brings joy for a shorter time than the last.

sections.heading: More Than Cleaning
paragraphs: Yet the answer to the question “why?” can not only be lost; it can also be found. In one of their articles, Amy Wrzesniewski and Jane Dutton described conversations with people who cleaned the rooms of a large hospital. Formally they all had the same duties: mopping floors, emptying bins, disinfecting and changing bed linen, day after day and room after room. Some of them described their work in exactly those terms, as a simple, thankless job to be endured somehow until the end of the shift.

The others, however, saw something more in their work: they felt part of the team that was healing patients. They knew which family needed a few words of encouragement and who would welcome a moment of ordinary conversation. One man said that he had stopped mopping the floor when a patient recovering from major surgery was slowly walking down the corridor to regain his strength. One woman worked on a ward where patients with brain injuries lay for months on end, often in a coma. Every so often she brought pictures from another room into the patients’ rooms, hoping it would give them a sense that something was moving forward.

The researchers called this phenomenon job crafting. The position and the duties stayed the same, but these people gave a different answer to the question of who they were doing it all for, and that answer was followed by concrete, if small, gestures. They had not been given this approach to work along with their uniforms. They developed it themselves, day after day, at the bedsides of complete strangers.

The puzzle experiment and the stories from the hospital corridors show that motivation is shaped by various things. An external reward can weaken our own desire to act, and meaning in work can be found even when its formal scope does not change. The question “why?” is easily drowned out, but it is also possible to find a new answer to it.

sections.heading: Eight Times “For Me”
paragraphs: The fullest portrait of a person who has everything and yet cannot find an answer to the question “why?” is found in the second chapter of Ecclesiastes. The author introduces himself as the son of David and king in Jerusalem (Ecclesiastes 1:1), which is why tradition identifies him with Solomon, a ruler famous for his wealth. The Hebrew name Qoheleth, by which he calls himself, is related to the Hebrew word for an assembly and is sometimes translated as speaker or teacher, someone who addresses those gathered; the BSB renders it “the Teacher”. In this chapter he carries out a kind of experiment on himself: one by one, he tests what a person can fill their days with and what is ultimately left of these attempts.

The list is impressive. It includes houses and vineyards, gardens and parks full of fruit trees, and reservoirs for watering young groves. Add to that herds and flocks such as no one in Jerusalem had owned before him, silver and gold, and finally male and female singers (Ecclesiastes 2:4-8). The Teacher admits that he denied himself nothing and that his work gave him joy (Ecclesiastes 2:10). These are the words of a man of action who laid out gardens and raised buildings, so it is easy to picture those building sites: stonemasons at the walls and water flowing into the new reservoirs in the heat.

Reading a translation, it is easy to miss an important detail. In the Hebrew original of these five verses the short word “li” (לִי), meaning “for me” or “for myself”, appears no fewer than eight times. It could be rendered roughly like this: I built houses for myself, I planted vineyards for myself, I made gardens for myself, I gathered silver for myself. All these great works have a single beneficiary in this account. A moment later comes the sentence that closes the whole list: “Yet when I considered all the works that my hands had accomplished and what I had toiled to achieve, I found everything to be futile, a pursuit of the wind” (Ecclesiastes 2:11).

The Teacher enjoyed his work day by day, and yet something broke inside him when it came to taking stock. The Hebrew word that the BSB renders as “futile” literally means vapor or breath: something that disperses before we can grasp it. Then he adds one more bitter thought: everything he has achieved will pass to a successor, and who knows whether that man will be wise or foolish (Ecclesiastes 2:18-19).

Two chapters later we find a sketch of a lonely man who has neither son nor brother, yet works without rest and greedily accumulates wealth. At some point this man asks himself: “For whom do I toil and bereave my soul of enjoyment?” The Teacher calls his situation futile and miserable, because work with no one to receive it slowly eats a life away from within (Ecclesiastes 4:8-9).

Toward the end of the second chapter, however, right after this bitter reckoning, comes a sentence that changes the direction of the story: “Nothing is better for a man than to eat and drink and enjoy his work” (Ecclesiastes 2:24). The Teacher adds at once that he has come to see where this satisfaction comes from: it is a gift “from the hand of God”. Earlier his own achievements seemed as fleeting as vapor; now he sees that the ability to find joy in work is a gift. For us, too, this is an encouragement to ask whom the fruit of our labor actually serves.

sections.heading: Work That Serves Someone
paragraphs: What does this mean for someone who will open a laptop or put on a hard hat tomorrow morning? Above all, that it is easier to find strength for work when we see whom it serves, and when there is a real face behind the task. Fair pay, of course, remains a matter of justice, and no sensible person dismisses it, but the strength to get through a difficult Tuesday comes from something quite different from an hourly rate.

In the Bible, work appears already in the garden, before the Fall, as a task entrusted to human beings: God places the man in Eden “to cultivate and keep it” (Genesis 2:15). Jesus probably did manual work for most of His adult life, and His neighbors in Nazareth knew Him simply as the carpenter (Mark 6:3). The Teacher fills in this picture from the other side. Joy in work is a gift, and a gift always has a giver. And the fruit of work usually has a recipient too. God gives you a day of work, and what you do with it can reach other people through your hands.

You can rarely change your job overnight. Far more often, though, you can notice whom your work serves, just as the cleaning staff in that hospital did. A spreadsheet can help someone receive their pay on time, and well-written code can make for a quiet evening without a system failure. A clean stairwell makes it easier for a neighbor to carry in her shopping, and a marked test helps a child see what they have already learned. If you cannot see anyone at all who benefits from your work, that too is an important signal. It is worth talking then with someone who can help you, before your enthusiasm dies out completely.

This idea has its limits, though. A sense of meaning does not justify poor working conditions. A company that talks a great deal about its mission but does not pay for overtime is trying to replace fair wages with lofty slogans. Looking for the person your work serves does not mean agreeing to everything. Sometimes the most honest answer to the question “Who am I doing this for?” turns out to be changing jobs.

Only at the height of his success did the Teacher begin to take stock of his achievements, after building houses, laying out gardens and making reservoirs. You can ask yourself “Who am I doing this for?” today, over an ordinary task, before you commit yourself to something more time-consuming.

questions: Who am I really doing the things I do most often for?
challenge: **In your thoughts.** Choose one task waiting for you today that you dislike. Complete the sentence “I am doing this for…” with a specific person in mind. Picture their face and think for a moment about what exactly will change in their day if you do this task well.

**In action.** Think of someone whose work makes your life easier, though you rarely notice it. It might be the receptionist at the front desk, the driver of your morning bus, the IT person at work, or whoever cleans your stairwell. Go up to that person today or send them a message, and tell them specifically what their work changes in your day. One genuine sentence is quite enough. People find strength more easily when they can see who their work is for, and you can show them in ten seconds. If you don’t meet anyone like that today, leave a thank-you note somewhere this person is sure to find it.
